title: Olinia Has the Formula to Succeed in Latin America, Capuano Tripp Says
author: Laura Poy Solano
content:
_This article by[Laura Poy
Solano](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Laura%20Poy%20Solano) originally
appeared in the [October 19, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/19/politica/olinia-tiene-
la-formula-para-triunfar-en-al-capuano-tripp), Mexico's premier left wing
daily newspaper._

Mexico has a winning formula, said Roberto Capuano Tripp, director and
coordinator of the project to develop the first electric minivehicle in
Mexico, called _Olinia_. The goal is to produce **up to 50,000 vehicles a
year** in the country, although in a first stage it will be 15,000. With this,
the aim is to serve a market segment intended for the transport of people and
goods over short distances and at low speed.

In an interview with _La Jornada_ , he explained that “we made a strategic
decision because we believe the best way to achieve that goal is to be able to
create a company that can count on the support of the State, but that operates
like a private company, that has its agility.”

For this reason, as of this week, the Secretariat of Science, Humanities,
Technology and Innovation (Secihti) launched, with the advice of Nacional
Financiera, the call to select investor partners, national and foreign, with
whom it seeks to constitute Sociedad Olinia.

With this effort, said the former director of Mexico City's Metrobús, the aim
is to create **the first Mexican automaker** dedicated to manufacturing,
distributing and marketing the minivehicles developed by the project, which
currently has three products: _Olinia 1_ , for passenger transport, as well as
_Olinia 2_ and _Olinia Van_ , intended for cargo transport. These vehicles
will go on the market with various levels of equipment and an average price
starting at 150,000 pesos.

The call seeks to raise **950 million pesos** to constitute a company that
does not currently exist. “We are going to capitalize it with the money we
raise, and when the company is constituted, the government will have **no less
than 33 percent and no more than 49 percent** of the company's total shares,”
he stated.

The rest of the shares, between 50.1 and 66 percent, he indicated, “will be in
the hands of private capital. And also, in the formula for gathering those
resources, foreign capital may be allowed, but no more than 33 percent of the
total, that is, between what the government and the Mexican investor will
have, the company will have at least 66 percent national capital.”

He asserted that one of the factors that may be of greatest interest to the
future capital partners is that the first stage, the one with the greatest
uncertainty and risk, corresponding to the development of the vehicle, has
already been overcome. Now, he explained, there is a model whose blueprints
are ready for industrialization.

> There is a significant leap in risk that a private investor generally does
> not assume. In fact, I think that is why we have not achieved a national
> vehicle company. We are the seventh-largest car manufacturer in the world,
> and the only one among the seven that does not have its own brand.
>
> Roberto Capuano Tripp

What we are seeking, he asserted, “is help to achieve what we in government do
not know how to do, which is to market, sell, distribute a product and provide
a service as is done in many companies very successfully in the Mexican
economy. We want to focus on what we are good at.”

Capuano Tripp recalled that the Mexican government invested **127 million
pesos** in the entire process of developing the Olinia prototypes. In
particular, he highlighted the work carried out by scientists, researchers and
engineers from universities and public research centers in at least 20 states.

He added that the goal is for the Olinia company to be able to open markets
not only in Mexico, but also in other Latin American countries. By 2030, it is
expected to be present in nations of the region that share the same mobility
challenges as Mexico.

He stated that the priority is for minimobility in the country to “grow with
the best conditions of quality and safety for its users.”
